provenance.source: Olympiad / First Law Energy Conservation Archive

questions.stem: An ideal gas enclosed in a cylinder with a frictionless movable piston absorbs $Q = 750\text{ J}$ of heat from an external burner. Simultaneously, the gas expands against an external pressure and performs $W = 450\text{ J}$ of work on the piston. What is the change in the internal energy $\Delta U$ of the gas during this expansion?

system_parameters.law: First Law of Thermodynamics: Delta U = Q - W

options.A: $\Delta U = +300\text{ J}$ (internal energy increases by $300\text{ J}$)
options.B: $\Delta U = +1200\text{ J}$ (internal energy increases by $1200\text{ J}$)
options.C: $\Delta U = -300\text{ J}$ (internal energy decreases by $300\text{ J}$)
options.D: $\Delta U = 0\text{ J}$ (internal energy is invariant in all thermodynamic expansions)

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Applying the First Law of Thermodynamics Delta U = Q - W with standard IUPAC/physics sign conventions: Q = +750 J, W = +450 J => Delta U = 750 - 450 = +300 J.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires applying energy conservation and sign conventions across coupled heat and work channels.

A.diagnostic: Correct: By the First Law of Thermodynamics, Delta U = Q - W, where Q is heat added to the gas (+750 J) and W is work done by the gas on the surroundings (+450 J). Thus, Delta U = (+750 J) - (+450 J) = +300 J. The internal energy increases by exactly 300 J.

B.diagnostic: Sign convention confusion: added work instead of subtracting (750 + 450 = 1200 J), confusing work done BY the gas with work done ON the gas.

C.diagnostic: Sign inversion error: calculated 450 - 750 = -300 J, inverting the thermodynamic direction.

D.diagnostic: Isothermal confusion: assumed internal energy is always constant in any expansion, confusing general expansion with an isothermal process.

progressive_hints.title: First Law Statement
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the mathematical equation for the First Law of Thermodynamics?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: The First Law of Thermodynamics is the statement of conservation of energy: $\Delta U = Q - W$, where $Q$ is heat added to the system and $W$ is work done by the system.

progressive_hints.title: Determine Signs of $Q$ and $W$
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Are $Q$ and $W$ positive or negative here?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Heat enters the gas $\implies Q = +750\text{ J}$. The gas expands and does work on the surroundings $\implies W = +450\text{ J}$.

progressive_hints.title: Calculate Internal Energy Change
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is $\Delta U = Q - W$?

reasoning_ladder.understand: Calculate the change in internal energy $\Delta U$ of an expanding ideal gas using the First Law of Thermodynamics.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Heat input $Q = +750\text{ J}$. Work performed by gas $W = +450\text{ J}$. Change in internal energy $\Delta U$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: First Law of Thermodynamics (Energy Conservation): $\Delta U = Q - W$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Out of 750 J of heat energy absorbed, 450 J leaves the system as mechanical work on the piston, and the remaining 300 J is stored inside the gas as increased microscopic kinetic energy (raising its temperature).

derivation_steps: State the First Law of Thermodynamics: $\Delta U = Q - W$.
Assign signs based on physical process: $Q = +750\text{ J}$ (heat absorbed), $W = +450\text{ J}$ (work done by gas).
Substitute into conservation equation: $\Delta U = 750\text{ J} - 450\text{ J}$.
Compute final result: $\Delta U = +300\text{ J}$.

limiting_cases.expected: Delta U = 0 J (all heat converted to work, temperature constant)
Delta U = Q = +750 J (all heat stored as internal energy)

independent_check.quick_check: Deposit $\$750$, spend $\$450$ on work $\implies$ balance increases by $\$300$. Exactly $\Delta U = +300\text{ J}$.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: If work had been done ON the gas (compression with $W = -450\text{ J}$), $\Delta U$ would be $750 - (-450) = +1200\text{ J}$. But the gas EXPANDED, so it lost 450 J to mechanical work. $\Delta U = +300\text{ J}$.
independent_check.watch_out: Be vigilant about sign conventions! In physics, $W$ is work done BY the gas ($\Delta U = Q - W$). In chemistry, $W_{\text{chem}}$ is work done ON the gas ($\Delta U = Q + W_{\text{chem}}$). Both give the exact same physical result $\Delta U = +300\text{ J}$.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: THERMO-07 (First Law of Thermodynamics)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: An ideal gas undergoes a closed thermodynamic cycle $A \to B \to C \to A$ on a $P$-$V$ indicator diagram, returning precisely to its initial thermodynamic state $A$. What is the net change in internal energy $\Delta U_{\text{cycle}}$ over the complete closed cycle, and what is the relationship between net work done $W_{\text{net}}$ and net heat absorbed $Q_{\text{net}}$?

system_parameters.process: closed thermodynamic cycle returning to initial state A
system_parameters.variable_type: internal energy U is a state function

options.A: $\Delta U_{\text{cycle}} = 0\text{ J}$ because internal energy is an exact state function; consequently, the First Law requires $W_{\text{net}} = Q_{\text{net}}$ identically
options.B: $\Delta U_{\text{cycle}} > 0\text{ J}$ because gas always accumulates heat over a cycle
options.C: $\Delta U_{\text{cycle}} = W_{\text{net}} + Q_{\text{net}}$; internal energy changes by twice the area enclosed
options.D: $W_{\text{net}} = 0\text{ J}$ for all closed cycles because displacement returns to the starting point

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Modeling state function cyclic invariance: because U depends solely on equilibrium state variables (P, V, T), the closed loop integral oint dU = 0 => Delta U_cycle = 0, which enforces W_net = Q_net via the First Law.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires formal thermodynamic model proof connecting state function path-independence with cyclic energy conversion.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Internal energy U is a state function—its value depends solely on the current thermodynamic state (P, V, T), not on the path history. For any process that returns the system to its initial state, oint dU = U_A - U_A = 0 identically. By the First Law of Thermodynamics, Delta U = Q_net - W_net => 0 = Q_net - W_net => W_net = Q_net. The net mechanical work performed by the cycle equals the net heat absorbed from the reservoirs.

B.diagnostic: Heat accumulation fallacy: confused heat (a path function) with internal energy (a state function), falsely claiming internal energy accumulates in a closed cycle.

C.diagnostic: Sign and state confusion: violated the fundamental definition of an exact differential.

D.diagnostic: Conservative force confusion: confused thermodynamic work (W = oint P dV = enclosed area != 0) with conservative mechanical displacement work.

progressive_hints.title: State Function Property
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Does internal energy $U$ depend on the path taken or only on the current state $(P, V, T)$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Internal energy $U$ is a state function. It depends ONLY on the current state. If a system returns to state $A$, its internal energy returns to its original value $U_A$.

progressive_hints.title: Cyclic Change in Internal Energy
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is $\Delta U_{\text{cycle}} = U_{\text{final}} - U_{\text{initial}}$ for a closed loop?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Because initial state is $A$ and final state is $A$, $\Delta U_{\text{cycle}} = U_A - U_A = 0$.

progressive_hints.title: First Law in a Closed Cycle
progressive_hints.prompt_question: If $\Delta U_{\text{cycle}} = 0$, what does the First Law $\Delta U = Q_{\text{net}} - W_{\text{net}}$ tell us?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $0 = Q_{\text{net}} - W_{\text{net}} \implies W_{\text{net}} = Q_{\text{net}}$. The net work done by the cycle equals the net heat absorbed.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Prove that the net change in internal energy over a closed thermodynamic cycle is zero and relate net work to net heat.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Closed path $\Gamma$ in $(P, V)$ space. Initial and final state $A$. State function $U(P, V)$. Path functions $Q, W$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Fundamental theorem of calculus for exact differentials: For any state function $U$, the cyclic line integral vanishes: $\oint_\Gamma dU = 0$. First Law: $dU = \delta Q - \delta W$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: $\oint_\Gamma dU = \oint_\Gamma \delta Q - \oint_\Gamma \delta W = 0 \implies Q_{\text{net}} - W_{\text{net}} = 0 \implies W_{\text{net}} = Q_{\text{net}}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: A cyclic heat engine does not consume its own internal energy to produce work; it acts as a steady-state transducer converting a portion of the net heat absorbed into mechanical work.

derivation_steps: State the property of an exact differential state function: $\Delta U = \oint_\Gamma dU = 0$.
Integrate First Law over the closed cycle: $\oint dU = \oint \delta Q - \oint \delta W$.
Substitute cyclic change in internal energy: $0 = Q_{\text{net}} - W_{\text{net}}$.
Conclude energy equivalence: $W_{\text{net}} = Q_{\text{net}}$.

limiting_cases.condition: Cycle area shrinks to zero (infinitesimal cycle)
limiting_cases.expected: Delta U = 0, W_net = 0, Q_net = 0

limiting_cases.condition: Carnot cycle, Otto cycle, or Diesel cycle
limiting_cases.expected: Delta U = 0 for any arbitrary reversible or irreversible closed cycle

independent_check.quick_check: Hiking analogy: If you hike up a mountain and return to the trailhead, your net change in elevation is ZERO ($\Delta h = 0$). Internal energy is thermodynamic elevation.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Ideal gas internal energy is $U = n C_v T$. Since initial temperature equals final temperature ($T_A = T_A$), $\Delta T = 0 \implies \Delta U = n C_v (0) = 0$.
independent_check.watch_out: While $\oint dU = 0$, the net work $\oint P dV$ is NOT zero! Work is the area enclosed inside the loop on the $P$-$V$ diagram.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: THERMO-07 (First Law of Thermodynamics)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: An ideal gas is taken clockwise through a closed rectangular cycle $A \to B \to C \to D \to A$ on a $P$-$V$ indicator diagram. State $A$ has $(V_1 = 1.00\text{ m}^3, P_2 = 300\text{ kPa})$. Path $A \to B$ is an isobaric expansion at $P_2 = 300\text{ kPa}$ to $V_2 = 3.00\text{ m}^3$. Path $B \to C$ is an isochoric depressurization to $P_1 = 100\text{ kPa}$. Path $C \to D$ is an isobaric compression at $P_1 = 100\text{ kPa}$ back to $V_1 = 1.00\text{ m}^3$. Path $D \to A$ is an isochoric repressurization back to $P_2 = 300\text{ kPa}$. What is the net mechanical work $W_{\text{net}}$ performed by the gas during one complete cycle?

options.A: $W_{\text{net}} = +400\text{ kJ} = +4.00 \times 10^5\text{ J}$
options.B: $W_{\text{net}} = +600\text{ kJ} = +6.00 \times 10^5\text{ J}$
options.C: $W_{\text{net}} = +200\text{ kJ} = +2.00 \times 10^5\text{ J}$
options.D: $W_{\text{net}} = 0\text{ kJ}$; work is zero because the gas returns to its initial volume

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Calculating net thermodynamic work as the enclosed area of the clockwise loop on the PV plane: W_net = (P_2 - P_1) * (V_2 - V_1) = (300 - 100) kPa * (3.00 - 1.00) m^3 = 200 kPa * 2.00 m^3 = 400 kJ.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires evaluating multi-step piecewise contour integral around a closed geometric trajectory.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Net work is the area enclosed by the clockwise cycle on the P-V diagram: W_net = (P_2 - P_1) * (V_2 - V_1) = (300,000 Pa - 100,000 Pa) * (3.00 m^3 - 1.00 m^3) = (200,000 Pa) * (2.00 m^3) = 400,000 J = 400 kJ. Because the cycle is traversed clockwise, the positive work of expansion along the upper path (W_AB = 300 kPa * 2 m^3 = +600 kJ) exceeds the negative work of compression along the lower path (W_CD = 100 kPa * (-2 m^3) = -200 kJ), giving net positive work W_net = +400 kJ.

B.diagnostic: Upper path only error: calculated only the expansion work W_AB = P_2 * Delta V = 300 * 2 = 600 kJ, forgetting to subtract the compression work W_CD on the return path.

C.diagnostic: Halving error: computed (1/2) * Delta P * Delta V as if the cycle were a triangle instead of a rectangle.

D.diagnostic: Path-independence fallacy: assumed work is a state function that vanishes on a closed loop, confusing thermodynamic work with state variables.

progressive_hints.title: Geometric Work on $P$-$V$ Diagram
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What geometric feature on a $P$-$V$ indicator diagram represents net work done in a closed cycle?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Net work is the AREA ENCLOSED inside the closed cycle loop. For a clockwise cycle, the net work is positive ($W_{\text{net}} > 0$).

progressive_hints.title: Area of a Rectangle
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What are the height $\Delta P$ and width $\Delta V$ of this rectangular cycle?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Height $\Delta P = P_2 - P_1 = 300\text{ kPa} - 100\text{ kPa} = 200\text{ kPa} = 2.00 \times 10^5\text{ Pa}$. Width $\Delta V = V_2 - V_1 = 3.00\text{ m}^3 - 1.00\text{ m}^3 = 2.00\text{ m}^3$.

progressive_hints.title: Calculate Enclosed Area
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the product $\Delta P \times \Delta V$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta P \times \Delta V = (2.00 \times 10^5\text{ Pa}) \times (2.00\text{ m}^3) = 4.00 \times 10^5\text{ J} = 400\text{ kJ}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Calculate the net work performed by an ideal gas around a clockwise rectangular thermodynamic cycle on a $P$-$V$ diagram.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Points: $A(1.0, 300\text{ kPa}), B(3.0, 300\text{ kPa}), C(3.0, 100\text{ kPa}), D(1.0, 100\text{ kPa})$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Contour integral for thermodynamic work: $W = \oint P dV = W_{AB} + W_{BC} + W_{CD} + W_{DA}$. Isochoric paths ($BC, DA$) have $dV = 0 \implies W_{BC} = W_{DA} = 0$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Because the expansion occurs at higher pressure ($300\text{ kPa}$) than the compression ($100\text{ kPa}$), the net area enclosed is positive, delivering 400 kJ of useful mechanical work to the environment.

derivation_steps: Express net cyclic work as piecewise line integral: $W_{\text{net}} = \int_A^B P dV + \int_B^C P dV + \int_C^D P dV + \int_D^A P dV$.
Evaluate isochoric segments: $W_{BC} = 0$ and $W_{DA} = 0$ since $dV = 0$.
Evaluate isobaric expansion: $W_{AB} = P_2 (V_2 - V_1) = 300\text{ kPa} \times 2.00\text{ m}^3 = +600\text{ kJ}$.
Evaluate isobaric compression: $W_{CD} = P_1 (V_1 - V_2) = 100\text{ kPa} \times (-2.00\text{ m}^3) = -200\text{ kJ}$.
Sum contributions: $W_{\text{net}} = +600\text{ kJ} - 200\text{ kJ} = +400\text{ kJ}$.
Confirm enclosed area formula: $W_{\text{net}} = (P_2 - P_1)(V_2 - V_1) = 200\text{ kPa} \times 2.00\text{ m}^3 = 400\text{ kJ}$.

limiting_cases.expected: W_net = 0 kJ (collapsed loop, zero enclosed area)
W_net = -400 kJ (work done ON the gas)

independent_check.quick_check: Area of rectangle: $\text{base} \times \text{height} = 2\text{ m}^3 \times 200\text{ kPa} = 400\text{ kJ}$. Verified.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: By Green's theorem in the plane: $\oint_{\partial \Omega} P dV = \iint_\Omega dP dV = \Delta P \cdot \Delta V = 200 \times 10^3 \times 2.0 = 400\text{ kJ}$. Identical result.
independent_check.watch_out: Clockwise cycle = positive work (heat engine). Counter-clockwise cycle = negative work (refrigerator/heat pump requiring work input).
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: THERMO-08 (Thermodynamic Work & PV Diagrams)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: An ideal gas is expanded from an initial equilibrium state $1$ ($P_1, V_1$) to a final equilibrium state $2$ ($P_2, V_2$) via two distinct quasi-static paths: Path $\text{I}$ is an isothermal expansion at $T_1$, while Path $\text{II}$ is a two-step path consisting of an isobaric expansion followed by an isochoric cooling. How do the work done ($W_\text{I}$ vs $W_\text{II}$), heat absorbed ($Q_\text{I}$ vs $Q_\text{II}$), and internal energy change ($\Delta U_\text{I}$ vs $\Delta U_\text{II}$) compare between the two paths?

options.A: $\Delta U_\text{I} = \Delta U_\text{II} = 0\text{ J}$ because internal energy is a state function, whereas $W_\text{II} > W_\text{I}$ and $Q_\text{II} > Q_\text{I}$ because work and heat are path-dependent
options.B: $W_\text{I} = W_\text{II}$ and $Q_\text{I} = Q_\text{II}$; all thermodynamic quantities are strictly path-independent
options.C: $\Delta U_\text{I} \neq \Delta U_\text{II}$ because the gas traveled along different curves on the indicator diagram
options.D: $W_\text{I} > W_\text{II}$ because an isothermal curve always encloses more area than any isobaric path

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Justifying that internal energy is a state function depending only on end states (Delta U = 0 since T1 = T2), whereas work is path-dependent area under the curve (W_II > W_I) which enforces Q_II > Q_I via First Law Q = Delta U + W.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires formal justification distinguishing exact differentials (dU) from inexact differentials (delta Q, delta W).

A.diagnostic: Correct: Since states 1 and 2 lie on the same isotherm (T_1 = T_2), and internal energy of an ideal gas depends solely on temperature, Delta U_I = Delta U_II = 0. However, work W = int P dV is the area under the P-V curve. Path II travels along the isobaric upper horizontal line at P_1 before dropping vertically, whereas Path I follows the curving downward hyperbola P = nRT/V. Clearly, the area under Path II exceeds Path I: W_II > W_I. By the First Law, Q = Delta U + W = 0 + W = W, which immediately requires Q_II > Q_I. Heat and work are path-dependent, while internal energy is path-independent.

B.diagnostic: Total path-independence fallacy: incorrectly classified work and heat as state functions.

C.diagnostic: State function denial: erroneously claimed internal energy depends on the path taken.

D.diagnostic: Area under curve inversion: incorrectly claimed an isothermal downward curve lies above a horizontal isobar.

progressive_hints.title: State Function vs Path Function
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Which of $\Delta U$, $Q$, and $W$ depends only on the initial and final states?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Only $\Delta U$ is a state function! For an ideal gas, $U$ depends solely on temperature. Because $T_1 = T_2$, $\Delta U_\text{I} = \Delta U_\text{II} = 0$ for BOTH paths.

progressive_hints.title: Compare Work Done Under the Curves
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Which path has greater area beneath it on the $P$-$V$ diagram?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Path $\text{II}$ expands at the initial high pressure $P_1$ (a high horizontal line), while Path $\text{I}$ drops along a downward curve ($P \propto 1/V$). The area under Path $\text{II}$ is visibly greater: $W_\text{II} > W_\text{I}$.

progressive_hints.title: Relate Heat via First Law
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Since $\Delta U = 0$ for both, how do $Q_\text{I}$ and $Q_\text{II}$ compare?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: By the First Law, $Q = \Delta U + W = 0 + W = W$. Therefore, since $W_\text{II} > W_\text{I}$, it must follow that $Q_\text{II} > Q_\text{I}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Compare the thermodynamic state change $\Delta U$ and path quantities $W, Q$ for two distinct expansion trajectories between the same endpoints.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Endpoints: $(P_1, V_1)$ and $(P_2, V_2)$ with $P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2$ ($T_1 = T_2$). Path $\text{I}$: $P(V) = \frac{n R T_1}{V}$. Path $\text{II}$: $(P_1, V_1) \to (P_1, V_2) \to (P_2, V_2)$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Internal energy of an ideal gas: $U(T) = n C_v T$. Since $T_2 = T_1$, $\Delta U = U(T_2) - U(T_1) = 0$ regardless of path. Work: $W = \int_{V_1}^{V_2} P(V) dV$. First Law: $Q = \Delta U + W = W$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: $W_\text{I} = n R T_1 \ln\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)$. $W_\text{II} = P_1 (V_2 - V_1) + 0 = P_1 V_1 \left(\frac{V_2}{V_1} - 1\right) = n R T_1 (x - 1)$, where $x = \frac{V_2}{V_1} > 1$. Since $x - 1 > \ln(x)$ for all $x > 1$, $W_\text{II} > W_\text{I}$. By First Law, $Q_\text{II} = W_\text{II} > Q_\text{I} = W_\text{I}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: While the net internal energy change is identically zero for both, Path II extracts more work from the surroundings and therefore requires more heat absorption to maintain energy balance.

derivation_steps: State the ideal gas internal energy theorem: $U = U(T)$.
Observe identical initial and final temperatures: $T_1 = T_2 \implies \Delta U_\text{I} = \Delta U_\text{II} = 0$.
Compute work along Path I (isothermal): $W_\text{I} = n R T_1 \ln(V_2 / V_1)$.
Compute work along Path II (isobaric + isochoric): $W_\text{II} = P_1 (V_2 - V_1) = n R T_1 (V_2/V_1 - 1)$.
Apply inequality $x - 1 > \ln(x)$ for expansion ratio $x > 1$: $W_\text{II} > W_\text{I}$.
Apply First Law $Q = \Delta U + W$: $Q_\text{I} = W_\text{I}$ and $Q_\text{II} = W_\text{II} \implies Q_\text{II} > Q_\text{I}$.
model_proof.final_expression: \Delta U_\text{I} = \Delta U_\text{II} = 0,\quad W_\text{II} > W_\text{I},\quad Q_\text{II} > Q_\text{I}

limiting_cases.expected: W_II / W_I -> 1, Q_II / Q_I -> 1
W_I = nRT ln(2) approx 0.693 nRT, W_II = nRT (2 - 1) = 1.000 nRT => W_II > W_I

independent_check.quick_check: $1.000 > 0.693$. Path II does $\approx 44\%$ more work than Path I and absorbs $\approx 44\%$ more heat. Both have $\Delta U = 0$.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Geometric inspection: The area between Path II and Path I is a positive curvilinear triangle with vertices at $(V_1, P_1)$, $(V_2, P_1)$, and $(V_2, P_2)$. Since this area is strictly positive, $W_\text{II} - W_\text{I} = \text{Area} > 0$.
independent_check.watch_out: Never say 'heat of a state'! Heat and work exist only during a process (they are path functions, inexact differentials $\delta Q, \delta W$).
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: THERMO-08 (Thermodynamic Work & PV Diagrams)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: An ideal gas at initial state $(P_0, V_0)$ can expand either reversibly and isothermally ($T = \text{const}$) or reversibly and adiabatically ($Q = 0$). How does the mathematical slope $\left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)$ of the adiabatic curve compare to that of the isothermal curve at the point of intersection $(P_0, V_0)$ on a $P$-$V$ diagram, and what is the physical reason for this difference?

options.A: The adiabatic curve is steeper by a factor of $\gamma$: $\left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{adia}} = \gamma \left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{iso}} = -\gamma \frac{P_0}{V_0}$, because as the gas expands adiabatically it does work without heat input, causing its temperature to drop simultaneously
options.B: The isothermal curve is steeper by a factor of $\gamma$ because temperature is kept artificially constant
options.C: Both curves have identical slope $-\frac{P_0}{V_0}$ at the intersection point because they share the same state $(P_0, V_0)$
options.D: The adiabatic curve has positive slope $\left(\frac{dP}{dV} > 0\right)$ because pressure increases during adiabatic expansion

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Differentiating isothermal P*V = C => dP/dV = -P/V and adiabatic P*V^gamma = C => dP/dV = -gamma*(P/V), proving the adiabatic curve is steeper by factor gamma = C_P / C_V > 1 due to simultaneous temperature drop.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires calculus differentiation of two distinct state paths and physical justification via cooling.

A.diagnostic: Correct: For an isothermal process: P * V = const => differentiating yields P dV + V dP = 0 => (dP/dV)_iso = -P/V. For a reversible adiabatic process: P * V^gamma = const => differentiating yields V^gamma dP + gamma * P * V^(gamma - 1) dV = 0 => (dP/dV)_adia = -gamma * (P/V). Since gamma = C_P / C_V > 1 (e.g. 1.40 for air), the adiabatic curve has a steeper negative slope by a factor of gamma. Physically, during adiabatic expansion the gas does work at the expense of its own internal energy (dQ = 0), so temperature drops, compounding the pressure drop.

B.diagnostic: Inverted slope ratio: claimed the isothermal curve is steeper, failing to account for adiabatic thermal depletion.

C.diagnostic: Equal slope fallacy: confused having the same coordinate point (P_0, V_0) with having the same derivative slope.

D.diagnostic: Positive slope absurdity: claiming pressure rises during unheated expansion violates basic Boyle-Charles physics.

progressive_hints.title: Differentiate Isothermal Relation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Differentiating $P V = \text{const}$ with respect to $V$, what is $\frac{dP}{dV}$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Product rule: $P + V \frac{dP}{dV} = 0 \implies \left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{iso}} = -\frac{P}{V}$.

progressive_hints.title: Differentiate Adiabatic Relation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Differentiating $P V^\gamma = \text{const}$ with respect to $V$, what is $\frac{dP}{dV}$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Product rule: $V^\gamma \frac{dP}{dV} + P \gamma V^{\gamma - 1} = 0 \implies \left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{adia}} = -\gamma \frac{P}{V}$.

progressive_hints.title: Physical Interpretation of the Ratio
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Why is the adiabatic slope steeper ($\gamma > 1$)?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: In isothermal expansion, heat enters to keep temperature constant. In adiabatic expansion, NO heat enters ($Q = 0$), so the work done comes from internal energy, causing temperature to drop ($T_2 < T_1$). Because both volume increases AND temperature drops, pressure plummets much faster!

reasoning_ladder.understand: Derive and physically justify the slope ratio of adiabatic versus isothermal curves on a $P$-$V$ plane.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Isothermal path: $P V = k_1$. Adiabatic path: $P V^\gamma = k_2$. Adiabatic index $\gamma = \frac{C_P}{C_V} > 1$. Common point $(P_0, V_0)$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Calculus of implicit differentiation for polytropic curves $P V^n = \text{const}$: $\frac{d}{dV}(P V^n) = V^n \frac{dP}{dV} + n P V^{n-1} = 0 \implies \frac{dP}{dV} = -n \frac{P}{V}$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: For isothermal process, $n = 1$: $\left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{iso}} = -\frac{P_0}{V_0}$. For adiabatic process, $n = \gamma$: $\left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{adia}} = -\gamma \frac{P_0}{V_0}$. Ratio: $\frac{(dP/dV)_{\text{adia}}}{(dP/dV)_{\text{iso}}} = \frac{-\gamma P_0 / V_0}{-P_0 / V_0} = \gamma > 1$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: The adiabatic curve is steeper by a factor of $\gamma$. For diatomic gas (air), $\gamma = 1.40$, so the adiabatic curve is $40\%$ steeper than the isotherm at the intersection.

derivation_steps: Formulate implicit differentiation for isothermal path $P V = \text{const}$: $d(PV) = P dV + V dP = 0$.
Isolate isothermal slope: $\left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{iso}} = -\frac{P}{V}$.
Formulate implicit differentiation for adiabatic path $P V^\gamma = \text{const}$: $d(P V^\gamma) = V^\gamma dP + \gamma P V^{\gamma - 1} dV = 0$.
Divide by $V^{\gamma - 1}$: $V dP + \gamma P dV = 0 \implies \left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{adia}} = -\gamma \frac{P}{V}$.
Take the ratio of slopes: $\frac{(dP/dV)_{\text{adia}}}{(dP/dV)_{\text{iso}}} = \gamma$.
Conclude that because $\gamma = C_P / C_V > 1$, the adiabatic curve is strictly steeper.

limiting_cases.expected: Adiabatic slope is 1.67 times steeper than isothermal slope
Adiabatic slope is 1.40 times steeper than isothermal slope

independent_check.quick_check: Bulk modulus $B = -V \frac{dP}{dV}$. Isothermal bulk modulus $B_T = P$. Adiabatic bulk modulus $B_S = \gamma P$. Since $B_S = \gamma B_T$, sound speed $v = \sqrt{B_S / \rho} = \sqrt{\gamma P / \rho}$ (Laplace correction to Newton's formula).
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Laplace's speed of sound in air: Newton assumed sound propagation was isothermal ($v = \sqrt{P/\rho} \approx 280\text{ m/s}$, $15\%$ too low). Laplace corrected it to adiabatic ($v = \sqrt{\gamma P/\rho} \approx 331\text{ m/s}$), proving the adiabatic slope is steeper by $\gamma$.
independent_check.watch_out: In an EXPANSION, the adiabatic curve lies BELOW the isotherm. In a COMPRESSION, the adiabatic curve rises ABOVE the isotherm!
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: THERMO-09 (Special Thermodynamic Processes)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A rigid, sealed steel tank of fixed volume $V = 0.050\text{ m}^3$ contains $n = 2.00\text{ moles}$ of an ideal monatomic gas at initial pressure $P_1 = 1.00 \times 10^5\text{ Pa}$. The gas is heated until its pressure triples to $P_2 = 3.00 \times 10^5\text{ Pa}$. What is the mechanical work $W$ performed by the gas, and how much heat $Q$ was added to the gas? (For a monatomic gas, molar heat capacity at constant volume is $C_V = \frac{3}{2} R$)

options.A: $W = 0\text{ J}$, and $Q = \Delta U = +1.50 \times 10^4\text{ J} = +15.0\text{ kJ}$
options.B: $W = +1.00 \times 10^4\text{ J}$, and $Q = +2.50 \times 10^4\text{ J}$
options.C: $W = +1.50 \times 10^4\text{ J}$, and $Q = 0\text{ J}$
options.D: $W = -1.50 \times 10^4\text{ J}$, and $Q = +3.00 \times 10^4\text{ J}$

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Applying the isochoric constraint dV = 0 => W = 0 J, then using the ideal gas equation Delta U = n*C_V*Delta T = (3/2)*V*Delta P = 1.5 * (0.050) * (2.00e5) = 15,000 J = 15.0 kJ => Q = Delta U = 15.0 kJ.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires multi-step state variable transformation converting P-V variables into internal energy change under rigid volumetric constraint.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Because the container is rigid, volume is strictly constant (dV = 0). Therefore, boundary work is identically zero: W = int P dV = 0 J. By the First Law, Delta U = Q - W = Q - 0 = Q. For an ideal gas with C_V = (3/2)R: Delta U = n * C_V * Delta T = n * (3/2 R) * Delta T = (3/2) * n R Delta T. From the ideal gas law at constant volume, n R Delta T = V * Delta P. Thus, Q = Delta U = (3/2) * V * (P_2 - P_1) = 1.5 * (0.050 m^3) * (3.00e5 - 1.00e5 Pa) = 1.5 * 0.050 * 200,000 = 15,000 J = 15.0 kJ.

B.diagnostic: Non-zero work error: invented work W = Delta P * V / 2 despite the container walls being completely rigid.

C.diagnostic: Inverted work and heat assignment: claimed heat is zero and work is 15 kJ, confusing isochoric with adiabatic.

D.diagnostic: Negative work confusion: misapplied compression work to a constant volume vessel.

progressive_hints.title: Work in a Rigid Container
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How much mechanical work is done by a gas inside a rigid container that cannot expand?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Thermodynamic boundary work requires moving a boundary ($W = \int P dV$). In a rigid container, volume is fixed ($dV = 0$), so $W = 0\text{ J}$ identically.

progressive_hints.title: First Law for Constant Volume
progressive_hints.prompt_question: If $W = 0$, what does the First Law say about heat $Q$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $\Delta U = Q - W = Q - 0 \implies Q = \Delta U$. All the heat absorbed goes entirely into increasing internal energy.

progressive_hints.title: Calculate $\Delta U$ from $\Delta P$
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How is $\Delta U$ related to $V \Delta P$ for a monatomic gas?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Since $n R \Delta T = V \Delta P$, $\Delta U = \frac{3}{2} n R \Delta T = \frac{3}{2} V \Delta P = 1.5 \times (0.050\text{ m}^3) \times (2.00 \times 10^5\text{ Pa}) = 15,000\text{ J} = 15.0\text{ kJ}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Calculate the work done and heat absorbed when an ideal monatomic gas is heated at constant volume.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Rigid volume $V = 0.050\text{ m}^3$. $P_1 = 1.00 \times 10^5\text{ Pa}, P_2 = 3.00 \times 10^5\text{ Pa}$. Monatomic gas: $C_V = \frac{3}{2} R$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Work definition: $W = \int_{V_1}^{V_2} P dV$. Since $V_1 = V_2 = V$, $dV = 0 \implies W = 0$. First Law: $Q = \Delta U + W = \Delta U$. Ideal gas internal energy: $\Delta U = n C_V \Delta T = \frac{3}{2} n R \Delta T$. Ideal gas equation of state: $\Delta(PV) = V \Delta P = n R \Delta T$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: $W = 0\text{ J}$. $\Delta U = \frac{3}{2} V (P_2 - P_1) = 1.5 \times 0.050 \times (3.00 \times 10^5 - 1.00 \times 10^5) = 1.5 \times 0.050 \times 2.00 \times 10^5 = 15,000\text{ J} = 15.0\text{ kJ}$. $Q = \Delta U = 15.0\text{ kJ}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Because no piston moves, zero work is performed on the environment; $100\%$ of the supplied thermal energy directly elevates the kinetic energy of the gas molecules, tripling the pressure.

derivation_steps: State the thermodynamic work integral: $W = \int P dV$.
Apply rigid boundary constraint: $dV = 0 \implies W = 0\text{ J}$.
Formulate First Law of Thermodynamics: $Q = \Delta U + W = \Delta U$.
Express internal energy for monatomic gas: $\Delta U = n C_V \Delta T = \frac{3}{2} n R \Delta T$.
Substitute ideal gas relation at constant volume: $n R \Delta T = V \Delta P$.
Compute heat absorbed: $Q = \frac{3}{2} V (P_2 - P_1) = 1.5 \times 0.050 \times 200,000 = 15,000\text{ J} = 15.0\text{ kJ}$.
model_proof.final_expression: W = 0\text{ J},\quad Q = \Delta U = \frac{3}{2} V \Delta P = 15.0\text{ kJ}

limiting_cases.expected: Q = 0 J, W = 0 J

independent_check.quick_check: Energy density of monatomic gas: $u = \frac{3}{2} P$. Change in energy density $\Delta u = \frac{3}{2} \Delta P = 1.5 \times 200\text{ kPa} = 300\text{ kJ/m}^3$. Total energy $\Delta U = u \times V = 300\text{ kJ/m}^3 \times 0.050\text{ m}^3 = 15.0\text{ kJ}$.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Temperature check: $T_1 = \frac{P_1 V}{n R} = \frac{100,000 \times 0.050}{2 \times 8.314} = 300.7\text{ K}$. Since $P$ triples, $T_2 = 902.1\text{ K} \implies \Delta T = 601.4\text{ K}$. $\Delta U = n (1.5 R) \Delta T = 2 \times 1.5 \times 8.314 \times 601.4 = 15,000\text{ J}$. Identical result.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT calculate $W = P \Delta V$ if $\Delta V = 0$! Without volume displacement, thermodynamic work is strictly zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: An inventor claims to have constructed a cyclic heat engine operating between a steam boiler at $T_H = 227^\circ\text{C}$ ($500\text{ K}$) and a cooling river at $T_C = 27^\circ\text{C}$ ($300\text{ K}$). The inventor claims that in each cycle, the engine absorbs $Q_H = 1000\text{ J}$ of heat from the boiler and produces $W = 500\text{ J}$ of useful mechanical work. Based on the Second Law of Thermodynamics and Carnot's theorem, is this claim physically possible?

options.A: No, the claim is physically impossible; the maximum theoretical Carnot efficiency between these reservoirs is $\eta_{\text{Carnot}} = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H} = 40\%$, but the claimed efficiency is $50\%$, which violates the Second Law of Thermodynamics
options.B: Yes, the claim is completely valid because $50\%$ efficiency is less than $100\%$
options.C: Yes, provided the engine uses helium gas instead of steam
options.D: No, because the First Law of Thermodynamics forbids producing more than $10\%$ work from heat

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Applying Carnot's theorem: maximum possible efficiency between two thermal reservoirs is eta_max = 1 - T_C / T_H = 1 - 300 / 500 = 0.40 (40%). Because claimed efficiency eta_claimed = W / Q_H = 500 / 1000 = 0.50 (50%) exceeds eta_max, the claim violates the Second Law.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires evaluating temperature conversions to Kelvin, computing thermodynamic efficiency bound, and adjudicating Second Law compliance.

A.diagnostic: Correct: First convert temperatures to absolute Kelvin: T_H = 227 + 273.15 = 500 K, T_C = 27 + 273.15 = 300 K. According to Carnot's theorem, no heat engine operating between two thermal reservoirs can be more efficient than a reversible Carnot engine: eta_max = 1 - T_C / T_H = 1 - 300 / 500 = 1 - 0.60 = 0.40 (40%). The inventor's claimed efficiency is eta_claimed = W / Q_H = 500 J / 1000 J = 0.50 (50%). Because eta_claimed (50%) > eta_max (40%), the engine violates the Second Law of Thermodynamics (Clausius/Kelvin-Planck statement) and is physically impossible.

B.diagnostic: First law only fallacy: believed any efficiency under 100% is allowed, ignoring the Second Law Carnot limit.

C.diagnostic: Working substance fallacy: Carnot efficiency eta = 1 - T_C / T_H is strictly independent of the working substance (helium, steam, air, etc.).

D.diagnostic: Invented threshold error: the First Law only requires W <= Q_H (energy conservation); it does not set a 10% limit.

progressive_hints.title: Convert Temperatures to Kelvin
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What are $T_H$ and $T_C$ in absolute Kelvin?

progressive_hints.title: Calculate Maximum Carnot Efficiency
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the theoretical upper limit on efficiency between $500\text{ K}$ and $300\text{ K}$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Carnot's theorem gives $\eta_{\text{Carnot}} = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H} = 1 - \frac{300}{500} = 1 - 0.60 = 0.40 = 40\%$.

progressive_hints.title: Compare Claimed Efficiency
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the claimed efficiency, and does it exceed the Carnot limit?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Claimed efficiency is $\eta = \frac{W}{Q_H} = \frac{500\text{ J}}{1000\text{ J}} = 0.50 = 50\%$. Because $50\% > 40\%$, the claim violates the Second Law of Thermodynamics and is physically impossible.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Evaluate whether an inventor's claimed heat engine efficiency violates the fundamental laws of thermodynamics.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Reservoirs: $T_H = 227^\circ\text{C} = 500.15\text{ K}$, $T_C = 27^\circ\text{C} = 300.15\text{ K}$. Claimed input $Q_H = 1000\text{ J}$, work $W = 500\text{ J}$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Carnot's Theorem (Second Law): The maximum theoretical efficiency of any heat engine operating between two thermal reservoirs is $\eta_{\text{Carnot}} = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H}$. First Law compliance: $W \le Q_H$ ($500 \le 1000$ satisfies First Law). Second Law test: $\eta \le \eta_{\text{Carnot}}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Although the engine does not create energy (it satisfies the First Law), it violates the Second Law by generating negative net entropy change in the universe. The claim is a Perpetual Motion Machine of the Second Kind (PMM2).

derivation_steps: Convert reservoir temperatures to absolute scale: $T_H = 227 + 273 = 500\text{ K}$, $T_C = 27 + 273 = 300\text{ K}$.
Calculate maximum Carnot efficiency: $\eta_{\text{Carnot}} = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H} = 1 - \frac{300}{500} = 0.40$ ($40\%$).
Calculate claimed thermal efficiency: $\eta_{\text{claimed}} = \frac{W}{Q_H} = \frac{500\text{ J}}{1000\text{ J}} = 0.50$ ($50\%$).
Compare values: $\eta_{\text{claimed}} = 50\% > \eta_{\text{Carnot}} = 40\%$.
Conclude violation of Second Law: Engine is physically impossible.

limiting_cases.expected: eta_Carnot -> 1.00 (100% theoretical efficiency only at absolute zero)
eta_Carnot = 0 (impossible to extract work from uniform temperature medium)

independent_check.quick_check: Clausius entropy inequality $\Delta S_{\text{univ}} = -\frac{Q_H}{T_H} + \frac{Q_C}{T_C}$. Here $Q_C = Q_H - W = 1000 - 500 = 500\text{ J}$. $\Delta S_{\text{univ}} = -\frac{1000}{500} + \frac{500}{300} = -2.00 + 1.67 = -0.33\text{ J/K} < 0$. Negative entropy production violates Second Law!
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Celsius error trap: If someone used Celsius ($1 - 27/227 = 1 - 0.119 = 88.1\%$), they would wrongly accept the claim! This proves why Kelvin MUST be used.
independent_check.watch_out: Never use Celsius temperatures in $\eta = 1 - T_C / T_H$! $T$ must always be in Kelvin.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: Which of the following statements correctly expresses the physical equivalence between the Kelvin-Planck statement and the Clausius statement of the Second Law of Thermodynamics?

system_parameters.kelvin_planck: No cyclic process can convert heat completely into work without rejecting heat to a cold reservoir
system_parameters.clausius: No cyclic process can transfer heat from a colder body to a hotter body without external work input
system_parameters.equivalence: Violation of either statement allows construction of a device that violates the other

options.A: They are logically equivalent: If a device could violate the Kelvin-Planck statement (converting $100\%$ of heat to work), that work could power an ideal refrigerator to transfer heat from cold to hot with zero net external work, thereby violating the Clausius statement
options.B: The Kelvin-Planck statement applies only to gases, while the Clausius statement applies only to solids and liquids
options.C: The two statements contradict each other and cannot be applied simultaneously
options.D: The Kelvin-Planck statement requires that temperature increases over time, while Clausius requires temperature decreases

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Justifying the logical equivalence of Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements by showing how coupling a 100% efficient heat engine to a standard refrigerator creates a self-acting heat pump violating Clausius.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires formal logical deduction proving bidirectional equivalence of two foundational thermodynamic postulates.

A.diagnostic: Correct: The Kelvin-Planck statement (it is impossible to construct a heat engine operating in a cycle that produces no effect other than the extraction of heat from a reservoir and the performance of an equal amount of work) and the Clausius statement (it is impossible to construct a refrigerator operating in a cycle that produces no effect other than the transfer of heat from a cooler body to a hotter body) are completely equivalent. If a hypothetical engine violated Kelvin-Planck (Q_H -> W with Q_C = 0), that work W could drive a standard refrigerator to pump heat Q_cold to Q_hot, resulting in a net spontaneous transfer of heat from cold to hot with no net work input, which violates Clausius.

B.diagnostic: Phase restriction fallacy: both statements are universal macroscopic laws applicable to all matter regardless of physical phase.

C.diagnostic: Contradiction fallacy: falsely claimed two harmonious foundational formulations of the Second Law contradict each other.

D.diagnostic: Monotonic temperature misconception: neither statement prescribes the global direction of temperature drift.

progressive_hints.title: Kelvin-Planck Statement
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Can a cyclic heat engine convert $100\%$ of absorbed heat into mechanical work without rejecting any heat?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: No! The Kelvin-Planck statement states it is impossible to extract heat from a single reservoir and convert $100\%$ of it into work without rejecting heat to a colder sink.

progressive_hints.title: Clausius Statement
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Can heat spontaneously flow from a colder object to a hotter object without external work?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: No! The Clausius statement states that heat cannot flow from cold to hot without external work being done on the system (a refrigerator must be plugged in!).

progressive_hints.title: Coupling the Two Devices
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What happens if you use the work from a 'perfect' Kelvin-Planck engine to run a refrigerator?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: The engine takes heat $Q$ from hot and produces work $W = Q$. That work runs a refrigerator, pumping heat from cold to hot. The net result of the combined system is heat moving from cold to hot with ZERO external work—violating Clausius! Therefore, violating one statement violates the other.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Demonstrate the mathematical and logical equivalence between the Kelvin-Planck and Clausius formulations of the Second Law.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Engine $E$: absorbs $Q_H$, produces $W$, rejects $Q_C$. Refrigerator $R$: absorbs $Q_C'$, requires work $W'$, rejects $Q_H'$.
reasoning_ladder.connect:
Logical equivalence proof: Statement $K \iff Statement C$. We prove this by showing $
eg K \implies 
eg C$ and $
eg C \implies 
eg K$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate:
Assume $
eg K$ (Kelvin-Planck is false): There exists an engine $E^*$ that converts $Q_H$ completely to work $W = Q_H$ ($Q_C = 0$). Now couple $E^*$ to a standard refrigerator $R$ that requires work $W' = W = Q_H$ to extract heat $Q_{	ext{cold}}$ from the cold reservoir and deliver $Q_{	ext{hot}} = Q_H + Q_{	ext{cold}}$ to the hot reservoir. Net heat extracted from cold reservoir: $Q_{	ext{cold}}$. Net heat delivered to hot reservoir: $Q_{	ext{hot}} - Q_H = (Q_H + Q_{	ext{cold}}) - Q_H = Q_{	ext{cold}}$. Net work exchanged with surroundings: $W - W' = 0$. The combined machine transfers heat $Q_{	ext{cold}}$ from cold to hot with zero external work, which is $
eg C$ (violates Clausius). Thus $
eg K \implies 
eg C$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Because violating Kelvin-Planck implies violating Clausius (and vice-versa), the two statements are logically isomorphic expressions of the irreversibility of natural thermal processes.

derivation_steps: State Kelvin-Planck: Impossible for cyclic engine to have $W = Q_H$ with $Q_C = 0$.
State Clausius: Impossible for cyclic refrigerator to pump $Q$ from cold to hot with $W = 0$.
Hypothesize a Kelvin-Planck violator engine $E^*$: $W = Q_H$.
Direct work $W$ from $E^*$ to drive a conventional Carnot refrigerator $R$.
Compute net energy fluxes of composite system: Net work is zero ($W - W = 0$).
Observe net result: Heat $Q_{\text{cold}}$ is transferred from cold to hot with zero net work.
Conclude that composite machine violates Clausius statement, proving logical equivalence.

limiting_cases.expected: Delta S_univ = 0 (reversible cycle equality)
Delta S_univ > 0 (irreversible entropy generation)

independent_check.quick_check: Reverse proof ($\neg C \implies \neg K$): Suppose a magical refrigerator transfers $Q$ from cold to hot with $W = 0$. Combine it with a standard engine that takes $Q$ from hot, does work $W$, and rejects $Q - W$ to cold. The cold reservoir has net change $+Q - (Q - W) = +W$. The hot reservoir has net change $-Q + Q = 0$. The composite machine takes heat from a single reservoir and turns it into work! Violates Kelvin-Planck.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Entropy formulation: Both statements are mathematically equivalent to the Clausius inequality: $\oint \frac{\delta Q}{T} \le 0$.
independent_check.watch_out: A refrigerator CAN transfer heat from cold to hot, but ONLY if you plug it in (external work $W > 0$ is supplied)! Clausius only forbids doing it with $W = 0$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: An insulated calorimeter contains $m_{\text{ice}} = 0.100\text{ kg}$ of ice at $0.0^\circ\text{C}$ and $m_w = 0.100\text{ kg}$ of liquid water at $0.0^\circ\text{C}$. Superheated steam of mass $m_s = 0.010\text{ kg}$ at $100.0^\circ\text{C}$ is bubbled into the calorimeter. Neglecting heat capacity of the vessel, taking $L_f = 3.34 \times 10^5\text{ J/kg}$, $L_v = 2.26 \times 10^6\text{ J/kg}$, and $c_w = 4186\text{ J/(kg}\cdot^\circ\text{C)}$, what is the final equilibrium state of the system once thermal equilibrium is reached?

options.A: Final temperature is $T_f = 0.0^\circ\text{C}$; the steam completely condenses and cools to $0^\circ\text{C}$, melting $80.2\text{ g}$ of ice, leaving $19.8\text{ g}$ of ice and $190.2\text{ g}$ of liquid water
options.B: Final temperature is $T_f = 100.0^\circ\text{C}$; all the ice melts and the entire mixture boils into steam
options.C: Final temperature is $T_f = 25.0^\circ\text{C}$; all ice melts and warms up to ambient temperature
options.D: Final temperature is $T_f = 0.0^\circ\text{C}$; all ice melts completely with zero ice remaining

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Synthesizing multi-phase enthalpy balances: steam condensation and cooling to 0°C releases Q_avail = m_s*L_v + m_s*c_w*100 = 22,600 + 4,186 = 26,786 J. Melting all ice requires Q_req = m_ice*L_f = 33,400 J. Because Q_avail < Q_req, final temperature is locked at 0°C with m_melt = 26786 / 334000 = 0.0802 kg (80.2 g), leaving 19.8 g ice un-melted.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires multi-phase multi-threshold energetic synthesis and piecewise thermodynamic phase elimination.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Calculate the maximum heat released by steam condensing to water at 100°C and cooling to 0°C: Q_steam = m_s * L_v + m_s * c_w * (100 - 0) = (0.010 kg * 2.26e6 J/kg) + (0.010 kg * 4186 J/(kg*C) * 100 C) = 22,600 J + 4,186 J = 26,786 J. Calculate the heat required to melt ALL the ice at 0°C: Q_melt_all = m_ice * L_f = 0.100 kg * 3.34e5 J/kg = 33,400 J. Since Q_steam (26,786 J) < Q_melt_all (33,400 J), the heat released by the steam is insufficient to melt all the ice. Therefore, the system remains locked at the phase coexistence temperature T_f = 0°C. Mass of ice melted: m_melt = Q_steam / L_f = 26,786 / 334,000 = 0.0802 kg = 80.2 g. Remaining ice: 100.0 g - 80.2 g = 19.8 g. Total liquid water: 100.0 g (initial) + 10.0 g (condensed steam) + 80.2 g (melted ice) = 190.2 g.

B.diagnostic: Steam dominance misconception: assumed steam must heat the mixture all the way to 100°C, ignoring that steam mass (10 g) is tiny compared to ice mass (100 g).

C.diagnostic: Blind algebra error: solved a linear sensible heat equation without verifying phase boundary thresholds.

D.diagnostic: Threshold neglect error: claimed all ice melts, failing to compare 26.8 kJ available against 33.4 kJ required.

progressive_hints.title: Heat Required to Melt All the Ice
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How much heat is required to melt all $100\text{ g}$ of ice at $0^\circ\text{C}$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $Q_{\text{melt, all}} = m_{\text{ice}} L_f = 0.100 \times 3.34 \times 10^5 = 33,400\text{ J}$.

progressive_hints.title: Compare Energies and Find Final State
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Does all the ice melt, and what is the final temperature?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Because $26,786\text{ J} < 33,400\text{ J}$, the steam cannot melt all the ice! The mixture remains at $T_f = 0.0^\circ\text{C}$. The mass of ice melted is $m = \frac{26,786}{334,000} = 0.0802\text{ kg} = 80.2\text{ g}$, leaving $19.8\text{ g}$ of ice un-melted.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Synthesize the multi-phase thermal equilibrium when $10\text{ g}$ of steam at $100^\circ\text{C}$ is mixed with $100\text{ g}$ of ice and $100\text{ g}$ of water at $0^\circ\text{C}$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Steam $m_s = 0.010\text{ kg}$ at $100^\circ\text{C}$. Ice $m_{\text{ice}} = 0.100\text{ kg}$ at $0^\circ\text{C}$. Water $m_w = 0.100\text{ kg}$ at $0^\circ\text{C}$. $L_v = 2.26 \times 10^6\text{ J/kg}$, $L_f = 3.34 \times 10^5\text{ J/kg}$, $c_w = 4186\text{ J/(kg K)}$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Maximum heat release from steam cooling to $0^\circ\text{C}$: $Q_{\text{steam}} = m_s L_v + m_s c_w (100 - 0)$. Total latent heat to melt ice: $Q_{\text{ice}} = m_{\text{ice}} L_f$. Coexistence test: If $Q_{\text{steam}} < Q_{\text{ice}}$, incomplete melting occurs at $T_f = 0^\circ\text{C}$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: $Q_{\text{steam}} = (0.010)(2.26 \times 10^6) + (0.010)(4186)(100) = 22600 + 4186 = 26786\text{ J}$. $Q_{\text{ice}} = (0.100)(3.34 \times 10^5) = 33400\text{ J}$. Since $26786 < 33400$, final temperature is pinned at $T_f = 0^\circ\text{C}$. Mass of ice melted: $m_{\text{melt}} = \frac{Q_{\text{steam}}}{L_f} = \frac{26786}{334000} = 0.08020\text{ kg} = 80.2\text{ g}$. Ice remaining: $100.0 - 80.2 = 19.8\text{ g}$. Total water: $100.0 + 10.0 + 80.2 = 190.2\text{ g}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Despite steam's enormous latent heat of vaporization ($2260\text{ kJ/kg}$), 10 g of steam cannot completely liquefy 100 g of ice; the system settles into a stable two-phase slurry at $0.0^\circ\text{C}$.

derivation_steps: Compute heat released by steam condensation: $Q_{\text{cond}} = m_s L_v = 0.010 \times 2.26 \times 10^6 = 22,600\text{ J}$.
Compute heat released by condensed steam cooling to $0^\circ\text{C}$: $Q_{\text{cool}} = m_s c_w (100) = 0.010 \times 4186 \times 100 = 4,186\text{ J}$.
Sum total heat available from steam: $Q_{\text{avail}} = 22,600 + 4,186 = 26,786\text{ J}$.
Compute heat required to melt entire ice mass: $Q_{\text{req}} = m_{\text{ice}} L_f = 0.100 \times 3.34 \times 10^5 = 33,400\text{ J}$.
Observe $Q_{\text{avail}} < Q_{\text{req}}$, proving phase coexistence at $T_f = 0.0^\circ\text{C}$.
Calculate mass of ice melted: $m_{\text{melt}} = \frac{Q_{\text{avail}}}{L_f} = \frac{26,786}{334,000} = 0.0802\text{ kg} = 80.2\text{ g}$.
Evaluate final inventories: $m_{\text{ice,final}} = 19.8\text{ g}$, $m_{\text{water,final}} = 190.2\text{ g}$.

limiting_cases.expected: Q_avail = 0.01247 * (2.26e6 + 418600) = 33,400 J = Q_req (all ice melts exactly, T_f = 0 deg C)
All ice melts and mixture warms to T_f > 0 deg C

independent_check.quick_check: Energy balance: Steam delivers $26.8\text{ kJ}$. Melting $100\text{ g}$ ice needs $33.4\text{ kJ}$. Shortage is $6.6\text{ kJ}$, meaning $\frac{6.6}{33.4} \approx 20\%$ of the ice remains un-melted ($19.8\text{ g}$).
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Specific enthalpy check with water at $0^\circ\text{C}$ as zero datum: Initial enthalpy $H_0 = m_s (L_v + 100 c_w) - m_{\text{ice}} L_f = 26786 - 33400 = -6614\text{ J}$. Since $H_0 < 0$, enthalpy is negative, meaning latent heat of fusion is incomplete. Remaining ice mass $= \frac{-(-6614)}{334000} = 0.0198\text{ kg} = 19.8\text{ g}$. Exact match.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT forget the heat released when the condensed steam water cools from $100^\circ\text{C}$ down to $0^\circ\text{C}$ ($4,186\text{ J}$)! Omitting it causes a $15\%$ error.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A straight bimetallic strip of total thickness $d = 2.00\text{ mm} = 2.00 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}$ is constructed by securely bonding two metal strips of equal thickness $d/2 = 1.00\text{ mm}$ and identical elastic properties. Strip 1 is made of brass with linear expansion coefficient $\alpha_1 = 19.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ K}^{-1}$, and Strip 2 is made of steel with $\alpha_2 = 11.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ K}^{-1}$. The strip is straight at temperature $T_0$. When heated uniformly by $\Delta T = 100.0^\circ\text{C}$, the strip bends into a uniform circular arc. What is the radius of curvature $R$ of the bimetallic strip, and toward which metal does the strip bend?

options.A: $R \approx 2.50\text{ m}$, and the strip bends toward the steel side (steel is on the inner concave surface)
options.B: $R \approx 1.25\text{ m}$, and the strip bends toward the brass side
options.C: $R \approx 5.00\text{ m}$, and the strip remains straight because internal stresses cancel
options.D: $R \approx 0.25\text{ m}$, and the strip coils into a tight spring

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Modeling bimetallic thermal curvature via strain geometry: L1 / L2 = (R + d/2) / (R - d/2) approx 1 + d/R = (1 + alpha_1*Delta T) / (1 + alpha_2*Delta T) approx 1 + (alpha_1 - alpha_2)*Delta T to derive R approx d / ((alpha_1 - alpha_2)*Delta T) = 2.00e-3 / (8.0e-6 * 100) = 2.50 m.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires developing a continuum differential curvature model linking differential thermal expansion to mechanical elastic bending.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Because brass has a higher coefficient of thermal expansion (alpha_1 = 19e-6) than steel (alpha_2 = 11e-6), brass expands more upon heating. To accommodate this differential strain without slipping at the bonded interface, the composite strip bends into a circular arc with brass on the outer (longer) convex arc and steel on the inner (shorter) concave arc. Geometrically, the ratio of arc lengths is L_1 / L_2 = (R + d/4) / (R - d/4) approx 1 + d/(2R). From thermal strain: L_1 / L_2 = (1 + alpha_1 * Delta T) / (1 + alpha_2 * Delta T) approx 1 + (alpha_1 - alpha_2) * Delta T. For strips of equal thickness and modulus, the radius of curvature is given by R approx d / ((alpha_1 - alpha_2) * Delta T) = (2.00e-3 m) / ((19.0e-6 - 11.0e-6 /K) * 100.0 K) = (2.00e-3) / (8.00e-4) = 2.50 m.

B.diagnostic: Concave-convex inversion: claimed the strip bends toward brass, forgetting that the more expanding metal must form the longer outer perimeter.

C.diagnostic: Zero curvature fallacy: claimed internal stresses cancel out bending, ignoring the fundamental operational principle of bimetallic thermostats.

D.diagnostic: Order of magnitude error: miscalculated millimeter to meter conversion, giving an unphysically sharp 0.25 m radius.

progressive_hints.title: Which Side is Outer (Convex) and Which is Inner (Concave)?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: When heated, which metal expands more, and must it form the longer or shorter arc?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Brass has higher $\alpha$ ($\alpha_{\text{brass}} = 19 \times 10^{-6} > \alpha_{\text{steel}} = 11 \times 10^{-6}$), so it expands more. The longer layer must be on the OUTSIDE (convex), bending the strip TOWARD the steel side (concave).

progressive_hints.title: Arc Length Geometry
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How are the arc lengths of the two layers related to the radius of curvature $R$ and total thickness $d$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: The outer layer has radius $R + d/4$ and the inner layer has radius $R - d/4$. Their length ratio is $\frac{L_1}{L_2} = \frac{R + d/4}{R - d/4} \approx 1 + \frac{d}{2R}$.

progressive_hints.title: Formula for Radius of Curvature
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Equating geometric strain to thermal strain, what is the formula and value for $R$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $R \approx \frac{d}{(\alpha_1 - \alpha_2) \Delta T} = \frac{2.00 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}}{(8.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ K}^{-1}) \times 100.0\text{ K}} = \frac{2.00 \times 10^{-3}}{8.00 \times 10^{-4}} = 2.50\text{ m}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Model the radius of curvature and bending orientation of a heated bimetallic strip.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Thickness $d = 2.00 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}$. Expansion coefficients: $\alpha_1 = 19.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ K}^{-1}$ (brass), $\alpha_2 = 11.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ K}^{-1}$ (steel). $\Delta T = 100.0\text{ K}$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Kinematic strain compatibility at bonded interface: Let the center-line of the brass layer be at radius $R_1 = R + d/4$ and steel at $R_2 = R - d/4$, subtending angle $\theta$. Arc lengths: $L_1 = (R + d/4)\theta$ and $L_2 = (R - d/4)\theta$. Thermal expansion: $L_1 = L_0 (1 + \alpha_1 \Delta T)$, $L_2 = L_0 (1 + \alpha_2 \Delta T)$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: $\frac{L_1}{L_2} = \frac{R + d/4}{R - d/4} \approx 1 + \frac{d}{2R}$. From thermal strain: $\frac{1 + \alpha_1 \Delta T}{1 + \alpha_2 \Delta T} \approx 1 + (\alpha_1 - \alpha_2) \Delta T$. Equating: $\frac{d}{2R} = \frac{1}{2} (\alpha_1 - \alpha_2) \Delta T \implies R \approx \frac{d}{(\alpha_1 - \alpha_2) \Delta T}$. Inserting values: $R = \frac{2.00 \times 10^{-3}}{(19.0 - 11.0) \times 10^{-6} \times 100.0} = \frac{2.00 \times 10^{-3}}{8.00 \times 10^{-4}} = 2.50\text{ m}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Because brass expands more, the strip bends away from brass and toward steel, forming a gentle arc of radius 2.50 m, which is used mechanically to open electrical contacts in thermostats.

derivation_steps: Express differential thermal strain between layers: $\Delta \epsilon = (\alpha_1 - \alpha_2) \Delta T$.
Relate geometric curvature to layer strain: $\epsilon_1 - \epsilon_2 = \frac{d}{R}$.
Equate thermal strain difference to geometric bending strain: $(\alpha_1 - \alpha_2) \Delta T = \frac{d}{R}$.

questions.stem: One mole of an ideal monatomic gas ($C_V = \frac{3}{2}R$, $C_P = \frac{5}{2}R$) is taken clockwise through a closed triangular thermodynamic cycle on a $P$-$V$ diagram consisting of three paths: Path $1 \to 2$ is an isobaric expansion at $P_0 = 2.00 \times 10^5\text{ Pa}$ from $V_0 = 0.010\text{ m}^3$ to $2V_0 = 0.020\text{ m}^3$. Path $2 \to 3$ is an isochoric cooling at $2V_0$ from $P_0$ down to $P_0 / 2 = 1.00 \times 10^5\text{ Pa}$. Path $3 \to 1$ is a straight linear return path on the $P$-$V$ plane from $(2V_0, P_0/2)$ directly back to $(V_0, P_0)$. What is the net mechanical work $W_{\text{net}}$ performed per cycle, and what is the thermal efficiency $\eta = \frac{W_{\text{net}}}{Q_{\text{in}}}$ of this heat engine? (Note: Along path $3 \to 1$, heat is released)

options.A: $W_{\text{net}} = 500\text{ J}$, and thermal efficiency is $\eta = 10.0\%$
options.B: $W_{\text{net}} = 1000\text{ J}$, and thermal efficiency is $\eta = 20.0\%$
options.C: $W_{\text{net}} = 250\text{ J}$, and thermal efficiency is $\eta = 5.0\%$
options.D: $W_{\text{net}} = 500\text{ J}$, and thermal efficiency is $\eta = 25.0\%$

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Synthesizing triangular cycle geometry with first-law heat accounting: W_net = (1/2)*Delta P*Delta V = (1/2)*(1.00e5)*(0.010) = 500 J; heat input occurs along Path 1->2 Q_in = n*C_P*Delta T = (5/2)*P_0*V_0 = 2.5*(2.00e5)*(0.010) = 5000 J => eta = W_net / Q_in = 500 / 5000 = 10.0%.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires multi-step synthesis of cyclic line integrals, isobaric enthalpy influx, and heat engine efficiency optimization.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Net work is the area of the right triangle on the P-V plane: W_net = (1/2) * base * height = (1/2) * (2V_0 - V_0) * (P_0 - P_0/2) = (1/2) * V_0 * (P_0/2) = (1/4) * P_0 * V_0 = 0.25 * (2.00e5 Pa) * (0.010 m^3) = 500 J. Heat is absorbed ONLY along path 1 -> 2 (isobaric expansion where both T and V increase): Q_in = Q_12 = n * C_P * Delta T = C_P / R * P_0 * Delta V = (5/2) * P_0 * V_0 = 2.5 * (2.00e5) * (0.010) = 5,000 J. Along path 2 -> 3, heat is released (cooling at constant volume). Along path 3 -> 1, both P and V decrease so heat is released. Thus Q_in = 5,000 J. Efficiency: eta = W_net / Q_in = 500 J / 5,000 J = 0.100 = 10.0%.

B.diagnostic: Omitted factor of 1/2 for triangle area: used W_net = Delta P * Delta V = 1000 J, erroneously doubling the work and efficiency.

C.diagnostic: Halved work error: calculated (1/8) P_0 V_0 = 250 J.

D.diagnostic: Used C_V instead of C_P: used Q_in = (3/2) P_0 V_0 = 3000 J, giving eta = 500 / 3000 = 16.7% or guessed 25%.

Identify heat influx path: Path $1 \to 2$ has $dP = 0, dV > 0$, so $Q_{12} = n C_P \Delta T > 0$.

Compute heat input value: $Q_{\text{in}} = 2.5 \times 2.00 \times 10^5 \times 0.010 = 5000\text{ J}$.

independent_check.check_it_another_way: Carnot bound check: $T_{\text{max}} = T_2 = \frac{2 P_0 V_0}{R}$, $T_{\text{min}} = T_3 = \frac{P_0 V_0}{R}$. $\eta_{\text{Carnot}} = 1 - T_{\text{min}} / T_{\text{max}} = 1 - 1/2 = 50\%$. Our cycle efficiency is $10\% < 50\%$, well within the Second Law bound.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT divide $W_{\text{net}}$ by $W_{\text{net}} + Q_{\text{out}}$! Thermal efficiency is strictly $\eta = W_{\text{net}} / Q_{\text{in}}$, where $Q_{\text{in}}$ includes only the positive heat absorbed.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: Which of the following rigorous thermodynamic arguments correctly derives and justifies Robert Mayer's relation $C_P - C_V = R$ for one mole of an ideal gas from the First Law of Thermodynamics and the nature of internal energy?

options.A: At constant volume, $W = 0$, so $dQ_V = dU = C_V dT$. For an ideal gas, $U$ depends solely on temperature, so $dU = C_V dT$ holds for all processes. At constant pressure, $dQ_P = C_P dT = dU + P dV = C_V dT + R dT$. Dividing by $dT$ yields $C_P - C_V = R$, physically representing the external expansion work performed against the atmosphere per degree temperature rise
options.B: Mayer's relation is an empirical approximation that holds only because gases have zero viscosity
options.C: At constant pressure, internal energy does not change ($dU = 0$), so $C_P dT = P dV = R dT \implies C_P = R$, while $C_V = 0$
options.D: $C_P - C_V = R$ is derived from Newton's third law of mechanical action and reaction alone

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Justifying Mayer's relation C_P - C_V = R by proving that dU = C_V*dT holds universally for an ideal gas (Joule's law (dU/dV)_T = 0), so isobaric heat must supply both internal energy C_V*dT and boundary work P*dV = R*dT.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires formal axiomatic derivation from the First Law and Joule's expansion invariance.

A.diagnostic: Correct: For 1 mole of an ideal gas: (1) At constant volume, dV = 0 => dW = 0, so dQ_V = dU = C_V dT. (2) By Joule's free expansion experiment, the internal energy of an ideal gas depends solely on temperature (dU/dV)_T = 0, meaning dU = C_V dT holds for ANY process, including isobaric heating. (3) At constant pressure: dQ_P = C_P dT = dU + dW = C_V dT + P dV. (4) Differentiating the ideal gas equation of state P V = R T at constant pressure yields P dV = R dT. (5) Substituting: C_P dT = C_V dT + R dT => C_P - C_V = R. Physically, C_P exceeds C_V by exactly the mechanical work R required to push back the atmosphere as the gas expands.

B.diagnostic: Viscosity confusion: Mayer's relation is an exact thermodynamic identity for ideal gases, independent of fluid viscosity.

C.diagnostic: Zero internal energy fallacy: temperature rises by dT during isobaric heating, so internal energy cannot remain constant (dU = C_V dT > 0).

D.diagnostic: Mechanics-thermodynamics confusion: Mayer's relation stems from thermodynamic energy conservation, not Newton's Third Law.

progressive_hints.title: Constant Volume Heat
progressive_hints.prompt_question: When 1 mole is heated at constant volume by $dT$, what is $dQ_V$ and $dU$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Since $dV = 0$, work is zero ($dW = 0$). By the First Law: $dQ_V = dU + 0 \implies dU = C_V dT$.

progressive_hints.title: Joule's Law for Ideal Gases
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Does $dU = C_V dT$ hold only at constant volume, or for any process of an ideal gas?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Because intermolecular potential energy is zero in an ideal gas, internal energy depends ONLY on temperature ($U = U(T)$). Therefore, $dU = C_V dT$ holds for ANY process, including isobaric heating!

progressive_hints.title: Constant Pressure Expansion Work
progressive_hints.prompt_question: At constant pressure, what is $P dV$ in terms of $dT$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Differentiating $P V = R T$ at constant pressure gives $P dV = R dT$. Substituting into the First Law: $C_P dT = dU + P dV = C_V dT + R dT$. Dividing by $dT$ gives $C_P - C_V = R$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Provide a rigorous first-principles derivation of Robert Mayer's relation $C_P - C_V = R$ for an ideal gas.
reasoning_ladder.represent: 1 mole of ideal gas. Heat capacities $C_V = \left(\frac{\delta Q}{\partial T}\right)_V$, $C_P = \left(\frac{\delta Q}{\partial T}\right)_P$. Gas constant $R$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: First Law of Thermodynamics: $\delta Q = dU + P dV$. Joule's Law for ideal gas: $\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T = 0 \implies dU = C_V dT$ universally. Ideal gas equation of state: $P V = R T$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: At constant pressure ($P = \text{const}$): $\delta Q_P = C_P dT$. Substitute universal internal energy: $\delta Q_P = C_V dT + P dV$. Differentiate equation of state at constant pressure: $P dV = R dT$. Combine: $C_P dT = C_V dT + R dT \implies (C_P - C_V) dT = R dT \implies C_P - C_V = R$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: At constant volume, all supplied heat raises temperature. At constant pressure, heat must both raise temperature ($C_V dT$) and perform boundary work ($P dV = R dT$) against the atmosphere. Thus $C_P > C_V$ by exactly $R$.

derivation_steps: Define heat capacity at constant volume: $C_V = \frac{1}{n} \left(\frac{\delta Q_V}{dT}\right)$.
Apply First Law at constant volume: $dV = 0 \implies \delta W = 0 \implies dU = C_V dT$.
Apply Joule's Law: For an ideal gas, $U = U(T)$ alone, so $dU = C_V dT$ holds identically for all paths.
Define heat capacity at constant pressure: $C_P = \frac{1}{n} \left(\frac{\delta Q_P}{dT}\right)$.
Apply First Law at constant pressure: $C_P dT = dU + P dV = C_V dT + P dV$.
Differentiate ideal gas law $P V = R T$ with $P = \text{const}$: $P dV = R dT$.
Substitute $P dV = R dT$: $C_P dT = C_V dT + R dT \implies C_P - C_V = R$.
model_proof.final_expression: C_P dT = C_V dT + P dV = C_V dT + R dT \implies C_P - C_V = R

limiting_cases.expected: C_P = C_V + R = 5/2 R, gamma = C_P / C_V = 5/3 approx 1.67
C_P = C_V + R = 7/2 R, gamma = C_P / C_V = 7/5 = 1.40

independent_check.quick_check: Mayer's historical calculation: Mayer calculated the mechanical equivalent of heat $J$ in 1842 by measuring $C_P - C_V$ for air and equating it to expansion work against the atmosphere, establishing the First Law before Joule!
independent_check.check_it_another_way: General thermodynamic relation for any substance: $C_P - C_V = T \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P$. For ideal gas $P = \frac{R T}{V} \implies \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V = \frac{R}{V}$, and $V = \frac{R T}{P} \implies \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P = \frac{R}{P}$. Thus $C_P - C_V = T \left(\frac{R}{V}\right) \left(\frac{R}{P}\right) = \frac{R^2 T}{P V} = R$. Identical result.
independent_check.watch_out: Mayer's relation $C_P - C_V = R$ is for ONE MOLE. For mass $m$ of specific heat capacities ($c_p, c_v$), it is $c_p - c_v = \frac{R}{M} = R_{\text{specific}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: Which of the following mathematical formulations correctly expresses the Clausius Inequality for any arbitrary closed thermodynamic cycle, and how does it establish that entropy $S$ is an exact state function for reversible processes?

options.A: $\oint \frac{\delta Q}{T} \le 0$, where equality holds strictly for reversible cycles ($\oint \frac{\delta Q_{\text{rev}}}{T} = 0$), proving that the line integral $\int_1^2 \frac{\delta Q_{\text{rev}}}{T}$ is path-independent and defines an exact state function $dS = \frac{\delta Q_{\text{rev}}}{T}$
options.B: $\oint \frac{\delta Q}{T} > 0$ for all natural cycles because heat always increases
options.C: $\oint \frac{\delta Q}{T} = \infty$ for reversible cycles because reversible processes take infinite time
options.D: $\oint \frac{\delta Q}{T} = -1$ universally for all gases

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Modeling the Clausius Inequality oint delta Q / T <= 0, proving that path-independence for reversible cycles oint dQ_rev / T = 0 defines entropy S as a state function, while strict inequality < 0 governs irreversible dissipation.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires setting up formal thermodynamic potential model linking Clausius integral to state-space topology.

A.diagnostic: Correct: The Clausius Inequality states that for any closed thermodynamic cycle, oint (delta Q / T) <= 0. For a reversible cycle, reversing the direction of traversal reverses the sign of delta Q, which requires oint (delta Q_rev / T) = 0. By Stokes' theorem / exact differential calculus, any cyclic integral of a quantity that vanishes on all closed paths is path-independent: int_1^2 (delta Q_rev / T) depends solely on states 1 and 2, defining the thermodynamic state function entropy S with dS = delta Q_rev / T. For irreversible cycles, internal entropy generation ensures oint (delta Q / T) < 0.

B.diagnostic: Sign error: positive cyclic integral would imply a perpetual motion machine violating the Second Law.

C.diagnostic: Infinitesimal rate confusion: confused infinite quasi-static process duration with integral value.

D.diagnostic: Arbitrary constant error: invented non-physical -1 value.

progressive_hints.title: Clausius Cyclic Integral
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the value of the cyclic integral $\oint \frac{\delta Q_{\text{rev}}}{T}$ for a reversible Carnot cycle?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: In a reversible Carnot cycle, $\frac{Q_H}{T_H} = \frac{Q_C}{T_C}$, so $\oint \frac{\delta Q_{\text{rev}}}{T} = \frac{Q_H}{T_H} - \frac{Q_C}{T_C} = 0$.

progressive_hints.title: Path Independence and State Function
progressive_hints.prompt_question: If a closed line integral vanishes ($\oint = 0$), what does that prove about the path integral between two states?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: If $\oint dF = 0$ for all closed loops, then the integral $\int_1^2 dF$ is STRICTLY PATH-INDEPENDENT. This means $F$ is a state function that depends only on the endpoints!

progressive_hints.title: Defining Entropy $S$
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What thermodynamic state function is defined by this path-independent integral?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: This defines ENTROPY $S$: $dS = \frac{\delta Q_{\text{rev}}}{T}$. For any irreversible process, entropy generation makes $\oint \frac{\delta Q}{T} < 0$, giving the universal Clausius Inequality $\oint \frac{\delta Q}{T} \le 0$.

reasoning_ladder.represent: Closed cycle $\Gamma$. Heat differential $\delta Q$ at local boundary temperature $T$. Reversible path $\Gamma_{\text{rev}}$, irreversible path $\Gamma_{\text{irrev}}$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Carnot decomposition: Any arbitrary reversible cycle can be decomposed into an infinite sum of infinitesimal Carnot cycles. For each infinitesimal Carnot cycle: $\frac{\delta Q_H}{T_H} - \frac{\delta Q_C}{T_C} = 0 \implies \oint_{\Gamma_{\text{rev}}} \frac{\delta Q_{\text{rev}}}{T} = 0$.

The value is identical for all reversible paths connecting states 1 and 2. Define $S_2 - S_1 = \int_1^2 \frac{\delta Q_{\text{rev}}}{T}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Entropy $S$ is elevated from an abstract integral into a fundamental geometric coordinate of thermodynamic state space, whose global change in an isolated system can never decrease.

derivation_steps: Decompose arbitrary reversible cycle into mesh of infinitesimal Carnot sub-cycles.
Sum Carnot heat ratios: $\sum_i \left(\frac{\delta Q_{H,i}}{T_{H,i}} - \frac{\delta Q_{C,i}}{T_{C,i}}\right) = 0$.
Take continuum limit to obtain closed loop integral: $\oint_{\text{rev}} \frac{\delta Q_{\text{rev}}}{T} = 0$.
Split closed loop into two arbitrary paths between states 1 and 2: $\int_{1,A}^2 \frac{\delta Q}{T} = \int_{1,B}^2 \frac{\delta Q}{T}$.
Conclude path-independence: Defines state function $S$ such that $dS = \frac{\delta Q_{\text{rev}}}{T}$.
Incorporate irreversible dissipative losses: $\oint \frac{\delta Q}{T} \le 0$ (Clausius Inequality).
model_proof.final_expression: \oint \frac{\delta Q}{T} \le 0,\quad dS = \frac{\delta Q_{\text{rev}}}{T}\quad (\text{exact differential state function})
